test_text.title: THE ROCKET - FROM EAST TO WEST

article.title: THE ROCKET - FROM EAST TO WEST

items.sentence_raw: The concept of the rocket, or rather the mechanism behind the idea of propelling an object into the air, has been around for well over two thousand years.

However, it wasn't until the discovery of the reaction principle, which was the key to space travel and so represents one of the great milestones in the history of scientific thought, that rocket technology was able to develop.
Not only did it solve a problem that had intrigued man for ages, but, more importantly, it literally opened the door to exploration of the universe.
items.explain: Q5: The passage says the reaction principle *'literally opened the door to exploration of the universe'* — **'exploration of the universe'** means **space travel**. So the greatest outcome was that **space travel became a reality**. The answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: An intellectual breakthrough, brilliant though it may be, does not automatically ensure that the transition is made from theory to practice.
Despite the fact that rockets had been used sporadically for several hundred years, they remained a relatively minor artefact of civilisation until the twentieth century.
items.explain: Q1: Students often think paragraph B is about the *first* rockets, but the passage says rockets *'remained a relatively minor artefact of civilisation until the twentieth century'*. This means they were not important for a very long time — they were **'undeveloped for centuries'**. So the heading is **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: Prodigious efforts, accelerated during two world wars, were required before the technology of primitive rocketry could be translated into the reality of sophisticated astronauts.

It is strange that the rocket was generally ignored by writers of fiction to transport their heroes to mysterious realms beyond the Earth, even though it had been commonly used in fireworks displays in China since the thirteenth century.
The reason is that nobody associated the reaction principle with the idea of travelling through space to a neighbouring world.
A simple analogy can help us to understand how a rocket operates.
items.explain: Q2: The passage starts with *'A simple analogy can help us to understand how a rocket operates'* and then describes the machine gun and boat. This whole paragraph explains the mechanism — **'how the reaction principle works'**. So the heading is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: It is much like a machine gun mounted on the rear of a boat.
items.explain: Q2: The passage starts with *'A simple analogy can help us to understand how a rocket operates'* and then describes the machine gun and boat. This whole paragraph explains the mechanism — **'how the reaction principle works'**. So the heading is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: In reaction to the backward discharge of bullets, the gun, and hence the boat, move forwards.
items.explain: Q2: The passage starts with *'A simple analogy can help us to understand how a rocket operates'* and then describes the machine gun and boat. This whole paragraph explains the mechanism — **'how the reaction principle works'**. So the heading is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: A rocket motor's 'bullets' are minute, high-speed particles produced by burning propellants in a suitable chamber.
The reaction to the ejection of these small particles causes the rocket to move forwards.
There is evidence that the reaction principle was applied practically well before the rocket was invented.
In his Noctes Atticae or Greek Nights, Aulus Gellius describes 'the pigeon of Archytas', an invention dating back to about 360 BC.
Cylindrical in shape, made of wood, and hanging from string, it was moved to and fro by steam blowing out from small exhaust ports at either end.
The reaction to the discharging steam provided the bird with motive power.
The invention of rockets is linked inextricably with the invention of 'black powder'.
items.explain: Q3: The paragraph begins by linking rockets to *'black powder'* and then talks about *'powder-propelled fire arrows'* in the thirteenth century. These are the very **first rockets** in history. So the heading is **v**.

items.sentence_raw: Most historians of technology credit the Chinese with its discovery.
items.explain: Q7: The passage says *'Most historians of technology credit the Chinese with its discovery'* — **'its'** refers to **black powder**. So the Chinese first invented black powder. The answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: They base their belief on studies of Chinese writings or on the notebooks of early Europeans who settled in or made long visits to China to study its history and civilisation.
It is probable that, some time in the tenth century, black powder was first compounded from its basic ingredients of saltpetre, charcoal and sulphur.
But this does not mean that it was immediately used to propel rockets.
By the thirteenth century, powder-propelled fire arrows had become rather common.

Q8: The passage says *'By the thirteenth century, powder-propelled fire arrows had become rather common'* and these were used by the Chinese. So the Chinese first used **rocket-propelled arrows for fighting**. The answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: The Chinese relied on this type of technological development to produce incendiary projectiles of many sorts, explosive grenades and possibly cannons to repel their enemies.
One such weapon was the 'basket of fire' or, as directly translated from Chinese, the 'arrows like flying leopards'.
items.explain: Q11: The passage describes the *'basket of fire'* as *'0.7 metre-long arrows, each with a long tube of gunpowder attached near the point'* fired from a basket. Drawing **B** shows multiple arrows with tubes near the tips in a basket-like holder. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: The 0.7 metre-long arrows, each with a long tube of gunpowder attached near the point of each arrow, could be fired from a long, octagonal-shaped basket at the same time and had a range of 400 paces.
items.explain: Q11: The passage describes the *'basket of fire'* as *'0.7 metre-long arrows, each with a long tube of gunpowder attached near the point'* fired from a basket. Drawing **B** shows multiple arrows with tubes near the tips in a basket-like holder. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Another weapon was the 'arrow as a flying sabre', which could be fired from crossbows.
The rocket, placed in a similar position to other rocket-propelled arrows, was designed to increase the range.
A small iron weight was attached to the 1.5m bamboo shaft, just below the feathers, to increase the arrow's stability by moving the centre of gravity to a position below the rocket.
At a similar time, the Arabs had developed the 'egg which moves and burns'.
items.explain: Q12: The passage says the Arab *'egg'* was *'stabilised by a 1.5m tail'* and fired using *'two rockets attached to either side of this tail'*. Drawing **E** shows an egg-shaped object with a long tail and two rockets on the sides. So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: It was not until the eighteenth century that Europe became seriously interested in the possibilities of using the rocket itself as a weapon of war and not just to propel other weapons.
items.explain: Q4: The key sentence is that Europe became interested in *'using the rocket itself as a weapon of war'* in the eighteenth century. The whole paragraph then gives examples of rockets used in battles — this is **'rockets for military use'**. So the heading is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: Prior to this, rockets were used only in pyrotechnic displays.

The incentive for the more aggressive use of rockets came not from within the European continent but from far-away India, whose leaders had built up a corps of rocketeers and used rockets successfully against the British in the late eighteenth century.
items.explain: Q9: The passage says the incentive for aggressive use came from India, whose leaders *'used rockets successfully against the British'*. This means the Indians first used **rockets as war weapons**. The answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: The Indian rockets used against the British were described by a British Captain serving in India as "an iron envelope about 200 millimetres long and 40 millimetres in diameter with sharp points at the top and a 3m-long bamboo guiding stick".
items.explain: Q13: The passage describes the Indian rocket as *'an iron envelope about 200 millimetres long... with sharp points at the top and a 3m-long bamboo guiding stick'*. Drawing **F** shows a long, pointed cylinder with a very long stick. So the answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: In the early nineteenth century the British began to experiment with incendiary barrage rockets.

The British rocket differed from the Indian version in that it was completely encased in a stout, iron cylinder, terminating in a conical head, measuring one metre in diameter and having a stick almost five metres long and constructed in such a way that it could be firmly attached to the body of the rocket.
items.explain: Q14: The passage says the British rocket was *'completely encased in a stout, iron cylinder, terminating in a conical head'* with a stick *'almost five metres long'*. Drawing **G** shows a thick cylinder with a cone-shaped head and a long stick firmly attached. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: The Americans developed a rocket, complete with its own launcher, to use against the Mexicans in the mid-nineteenth century.
items.explain: Q10: The passage clearly states *'The Americans developed a rocket, complete with its own launcher'*. So the Americans first invented **the rocket launcher**. The answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: A long cylindrical tube was propped up by two sticks and fastened to the top of the launcher, thereby allowing the rockets to be inserted and lit from the other end.
However, the results were sometimes not that impressive as the behaviour of the rockets in flight was less than predictable.
Since then, there have been huge developments in rocket technology, often with devastating results in the forum of war.
items.explain: Q6: The passage says *'Since then, there have been huge developments in rocket technology'* — **'since then'** refers to the time after the early nineteenth century, meaning from the late nineteenth century to now. So the greatest progress was made **from the late nineteenth century to the present day**. The answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Nevertheless, the modern day space programs owe their success to the humble beginnings of those in previous centuries who developed the foundations of the reaction principle.
Who knows what it will be like in the future?
